extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental scientists (Fellows of the Royal Society and similar readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting empirical observations and experiments in natural philosophy (including hydrostatic measures, anatomical experiments, meteorological registers, microscopy, and practical land/ water management), with emphasis on methods, repetition, and detailed description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic examination of solids and fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: The solids here mentioned were examined hydrostatically, by weighing them in air and water; but the fluids by weighing an equal portion of each in a glass holding about a quart. The numbers show the proportion of gravity of equal portions or bulk of these bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: weigh solids in air and then in water to obtain specific gravity; for fluids, weigh equal portions in a standard glass (~one quart). Use the proportion between water and substance plus the known weight of a cubic foot of water and the rule of three to compute the weight (or magnitude) of a cubic foot of the substance. This allows determining magnitude of irregular pieces by their gravity. Note and account for small experimental errors (e.g., glass weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometer register by parallel-line month-maps
rubrics_metrics.description: This register of the barometer is by a new and easy invention of observing the rise and fall of the mercury in the barometer, by parallel lines drawn from every decimal part of each month of its whole extent, marked by the wandering pricked line in the figure belonging to each month, like a map as invented by Dr. Lister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a visual, mapped register of daily barometer readings for each month (parallel lines for decimal parts) and a daily printed list noting the corresponding state of the weather (quarters of the wind E, W, N, S; rain or fair; frost or snow). The graphical/monthly-map format makes rise/fall patterns visible and supports better long-term interpretation and prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily, faithful meteorological recording across years and places
rubrics_metrics.description: In a printed list for every day in the year, is set down the corresponding state of the weather, as to the quarters of the wind... also as to the rain or fair weather, frost or snow, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: observe and record the weather every day (examples: Walter Merle's seven years of daily observations; Erasmus Bartholin's year). Keep consistent registers across multiple locations and years. Rationale: cumulative, repeated observations in diverse parts of the world will yield far more reliable and useful knowledge and improve predictive ability over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report experimental repetition and note errors for dependability
rubrics_metrics.description: The last experiment was tried with another quantity of quicksilver, which had been used in water in the preceding experiment, and this last is more to be depended on; as a small mistake, though here in the calculation allowed for, was found in the weight of the glass containing the quicksilver in the preceding trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat experiments when possible and report both original and repeat trials. Explicitly note any identified errors (e.g., mis-weighed glass) and how subsequent trials correct or confirm results. Use replication and transparent reporting to increase dependability of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description of experimental interventions and observed effects (anatomical experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of experiments on dogs listing procedures and findings: e.g., a mastiff bled 5 lb. Troy weight; ribs more brittle near vertebrae; needle into brain produced epilepsy-like behavior; tying six veins produced apparent choking reversed by loosening and bloodletting; injections of tallow into veins tried; observations on lacteals and valves in ductus thoracicus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting anatomical/physiological experiments, record specific interventions (amounts bled, arteries/veins tied, injections), immediate observable effects, differences in outcomes by site, comparative notes (across species or sides of body), measurements where possible, and any derived queries or corollaries regarding anatomy or function. Include both positive observations and negative claims (e.g., absence of lacteals from certain organs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopical observation protocol for salts/particles in fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of many particles in vinegar and wine (called 'the salt of the vinegar/wine') with distinct shapes: tapering figures, oval figures, hollow/boat-like forms, sharp or diaphanous particles. Methods included leaving samples open to air for hours to weeks, placing samples in narrow glasses, adding crab's eyes or powdered chalk to provoke changes, and killing/comparing small eels to gauge size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological steps: examine small drops under magnification after varying exposure times (hours, days, weeks); use standardized containers (e.g., 2-inch wide glass) and small added materials (crabs' eyes, chalk) to provoke or reveal particle formation; document particle shapes, size comparisons (e.g., relative to barleycorns or small eels), estimate counts (gross computations), and note changes over time. Report differences across sample types and experimental manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative, quantitative inference linking microscopic structure to macroscopic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: From microscopic salts in wine and vinegar the author infers sensory properties: 'These particles I take to be the sharp pungent matter, which causes the sense in the tongue, which we term sour... the pleasant relish of wine, consists in one sort tempering the other... that wine, having stood some time in the open air, loses its savour: namely, that many small salt particles are joined together, to make a few great ones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit links from observed microstructure (particle size, number, aggregation) to macroscopic qualities (taste, sourness, loss of savour), supporting claims with comparative observations (different wines, ages, manipulations). Where possible, quantify (counts/estimates) and describe aggregation dynamics (small particles joining to form larger ones) as evidence for sensory changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical diagnosis and remedies for bogs and loughs (land and water management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bogs arise from springs, moss, and want of clearing; quaking bogs form from tufted grass/roots; bottoms often of white clay/marl; draining (cutting deep trenches to reach original springs) will discharge vast quantities of water and cause bogs to subside; most bogs would well reward the expense of draining them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bogs by locating springs and examining bottom substrate; use drainage (trenches/vents) to lower water table and convert bogs into meadow or productive land, considering planting trees around drained loughs and converting residues to fish-ponds. Weigh cost against long-term value: while upfront expense may be high, drained bogs often repay costs. Document local hydrology and slope to determine feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific guidance for handling turloughs and lakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Turloughs (seasonal land-lakes) have holes from which water rises in winter and retires in summer; often hard to drain when encompassed by hills. To remedy overflow, make the passage (vent) as low as the bottom of the flat or, if necessary, sink the rivulet though this may require cutting through rock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For turloughs, locate natural vents or subterranean passages and lower the outlet to the flat's bottom to prevent winter overflow; when nearby rivulets fill flats, lowering the rivulet itself may be required (difficult when rocky). When possible, after lowering water, use residue for meadow or grain (especially rape) and plant trees for ornament and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of long-term, systematic local observation (case examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples cited of diligent observers: Walter Merle observed the weather every day of the month seven years together; Erasmus Bartholin observed the weather every day through the whole year 1671.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize disciplined, continuous observation as a methodological standard: daily logs maintained for years at the same place are valuable evidentiary resources. Encourage preservation of manuscripts/copies (e.g., Bodleian) and sharing records to build cumulative knowledge.
